$$ w\ge l_xy+l_yx-l_xl_y,\qquad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y $$
$$ w\le u_xy+l_yx-u_xl_y,\qquad w\le l_xy+u_yx-l_xu_y $$
The term **McCormick envelope** will mean this polytope. Its exact relation to the convex hull of the product graph is established by the local bilinear-hull result.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

derivations.claim: On the graph $w=xy$, subtracting the first lower plane from $xy$ gives $(x-l_x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting the second lower plane gives $(u_x-x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Subtracting $xy$ from the first upper plane gives $(u_x-x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting it from the second upper plane gives $(x-l_x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Thus every graph point satisfies all four inequalities.

If both widths are positive, put $s=u_x-l_x>0$, $t=u_y-l_y>0$, $X=(x-l_x)/s$, $Y=(y-l_y)/t$, and $W=(w-l_xy-l_yx+l_xl_y)/(st)$. The inequalities become $0\le X,Y\le1$, $W\ge0$, $W\ge X+Y-1$, $W\le X$, and $W\le Y$.

Every defining bound and McCormick inequality is affine in $(x,y,w)$. If two points satisfy one such affine inequality, their line segment also satisfies it by linearity, so the polytope is convex by [F2]. By step 1.1 every graph point lies in this polytope, and therefore each finite convex combination of graph points lies there by repeated segment closure [L1].

If $u_x=l_x$, the first lower and first upper inequalities force $w=l_xy$; all graph points satisfy the other inequalities by step 1.1. For any $y,y'\in[l_y,u_y]$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, the segment between $(l_x,y,l_xy)$ and $(l_x,y',l_xy')$ is $(l_x,\theta y+(1-\theta)y',l_x(\theta y+(1-\theta)y'))$, again on the graph. If $u_y=l_y$, the first lower and second upper inequalities force $w=x l_y$, and the same calculation with $x,x'\in[l_x,u_x]$ proves convexity. Thus either degenerate case gives the product graph itself.

In the nondegenerate case of step 1.2, set $\lambda_{11}=W$, $\lambda_{10}=X-W$, $\lambda_{01}=Y-W$, and $\lambda_{00}=1-X-Y+W$. Step 1.2 makes each coefficient nonnegative; their sum is $1$, and $(X,Y,W)=\lambda_{00}(0,0,0)+\lambda_{10}(1,0,0)+\lambda_{01}(0,1,0)+\lambda_{11}(1,1,1)$. Each vertex lies on $W=XY$, so every normalized polytope point is a convex combination of graph points.

If either width is zero, step 2.2 gives equality directly. If both are positive, the affine map in step 1.2 is invertible, and steps 2.1 and 2.3 prove both inclusions after normalization. These cases exhaust the ordered endpoint choices, proving equality of the original polytope and graph convex hull.

Suppose [[alg-bounded-mixed-integer-branch-and-bound]] returns a feasible incumbent with verified upper bound $U$ and a complete ledger of all nonempty terminal mixed nodes, each with lower bound $\ell_N$ valid on every feasible point in that node. Let $L$ be the least ledger bound. If $U-L\le\varepsilon$, then the incumbent $(\hat x,\hat z)$ satisfies
$$f(\hat x,\hat z)-\inf_{(x,z)\in C\cap(X\times Z)}f(x,z)\le\varepsilon.$$
If every terminal node is certified empty, then the mixed feasible set is empty. The conclusion applies both to the branch tree and to the fallback only when every bounded integer assignment has a complete continuous ledger.

derivations.claim: For each fixed $z\in\{0,1,2\}$, the square $(x-z/2)^2$ is nonnegative, so $F(z,x)\ge(z-2)^2/10$. The point $x=z/2$ belongs to $[0,1]$ and attains equality. Thus the exact fixed-integer minima are $2/5$, $1/10$, and $0$, respectively.

The fallback enumerates all three integer assignments and uses each exact square-completion lower bound with its attaining feasible point. Taking the least of the three lower bounds gives $L=0$, and the assignment $(z,x)=(2,1)$ gives $U=0$. The total gap is exactly zero.
Therefore $(2,1)$ is globally optimal and is a zero-gap mixed-integer certificate. The proof uses finite enumeration and exact values; it makes no complexity claim for larger integer ranges.
